info.name: LinkedIn Profile API
info.description:
# LinkedIn Profile API

Accepts a LinkedIn profile URL and returns the profile as structured JSON — name, headline, location, summary, positions, education, skills, certifications, languages and media.

Data is read from LinkedIn's internal Voyager API, the same endpoints linkedin.com's own single-page application calls, rather than by parsing rendered HTML.

**Base URL:** `https://linkedin.viral-engine.ai`

---

## Getting started

1. Select the **LinkedIn Profile API — Production** environment.
2. Send **Profile → Get profile by URL**.

No credential is needed unless the deployment is configured with API keys, in which case set `apiKey` in the environment and enable the `x-api-key` header.

---

## Rate limits

Three independent tiers, because they protect different things:

| Tier | Limit | Scope | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| New profile fetches | 5/min | Service-wide | Protects the upstream account |
| Per caller | 10/min | Per API key, else client IP | Stops one caller consuming the service |
| Service total | 20/min | All callers | Bounds total load |

**A cache hit contacts the upstream not at all, so it never consumes fetch budget.** Already-known profiles keep resolving at the full per-caller rate even when the fetch budget is exhausted.

Every `429` carries a `retry-after` header and a `retryAfterSeconds` field.

---

## Response conventions

- Every response carries a boolean `success`, so a client can branch on one field before reading anything else.
- `null` means "we looked and LinkedIn did not have it". Every array is always present, possibly empty, so a client never branches on `undefined` before iterating.
- Dates are structured `{ day, month, year }` with nullable parts, because LinkedIn stores month + year for most entries and sometimes only a year. A preformatted string would destroy that precision and impose one locale.
- `meta.missingSections` distinguishes "the member has none" from "we could not read it", so a consumer never records an absence that was really a failure.

---

## Timing

| Path | Typical |
|---|---|
| Cache hit | 30–80 ms |
| Live fetch, warm session | 1–7 s |
| Live fetch, cold session | up to ~10 s |

Set a client timeout of at least 30 s for live fetches.

---

Source: https://github.com/tchandrakar/tross-assignment

request.description:
Bypasses the cache and fetches from LinkedIn even when a fresh copy is stored.

This consumes one of the 5-per-minute fetch slots, so use it deliberately. Expect a multi-second response: a live fetch is roughly 1–7s warm, and up to ~10s if the browser session has to be established first.
Identical semantics to `GET /v1/profile`. Provided for clients that prefer not to place identifiers in query strings, where they end up in access logs and browser history.
Only member profiles (`/in/…`) are supported. Company and school URLs are rejected explicitly rather than misinterpreted as members — a silent misparse would return a confidently wrong profile.

item.name: Operations
item.description:
Health, quota, and the endpoints used to recover an upstream session.

**Note on shape:** `/health` and `/healthz` deliberately sit outside the `success`/`data`/`meta` envelope used by the rest of the API. They are probes consumed by orchestrators and monitoring rather than by API clients, and wrapping a liveness probe in an envelope would add a field every probe has to unwrap for no benefit.

request.description:
Service status, dependency health, and remaining quota across all three rate limit tiers.

Deliberately exempt from rate limiting: the endpoint that reports remaining quota has to stay reachable precisely when a caller is being throttled.

Two fields matter operationally:
- `pendingChallenges` — non-empty means the upstream is waiting on a verification code (see the Operations folder).
- `loginHealth` — non-empty means automatic re-authentication is failing.

console.warn('A verification challenge is awaiting a code — see Operations → Submit verification code.');

request.description: Liveness only. Touches no dependency, so an upstream problem cannot cause the platform to recycle an otherwise healthy container. Never rate limited.

Completes a pending upstream verification challenge.

LinkedIn challenges an unattended sign-in from an unfamiliar device or network — which a datacenter address is by definition. A challenge is bound to the browser session that triggered it, so discarding that session and signing in again only produces another challenge. The service therefore holds the browser open and reports the challenge on `/health`; this endpoint delivers the code to it.

The code arrives by email at the configured account. A mistyped code leaves the challenge open for another attempt; unanswered challenges are reaped after 45 minutes.

Machine-readable contract and rate limit behaviour.

**Note on shape:** `/docs/json` returns an OpenAPI document, whose shape the specification dictates, so it sits outside the `success`/`data`/`meta` envelope used by the API endpoints.

request.description: The OpenAPI 3.0 document, generated from the same schemas the service validates against — so the published contract cannot drift from the implementation. Interactive documentation is at `/docs`.

Run this repeatedly (Postman's Runner with 12+ iterations) to observe the per-caller limit.

The first 10 requests in any 60-second window return 400 — the URL is deliberately invalid, so nothing is fetched — and the 11th returns 429 with a `retry-after` header.

This exercises the limiter without consuming any fetch budget, because an invalid URL never reaches LinkedIn.
